content: Tetanus is a disease caused by bacteria known as Clostridium tetani. These bacteria are commonly found in soil, dust, and animal feces (manure). The bacteria typically enter the body through breaks in the skin, such as cuts, animal bites, or wounds. Importantly, tetanus is not contagious and cannot be transmitted from one person to another. A hallmark symptom of tetanus is the tightening of the jaw muscles, which can prevent the affected individual from opening their mouth, a condition often referred to as lockjaw. Other symptoms include painful muscle spasms, muscle stiffness, difficulty swallowing, seizures, headaches, fever, sweating, breathing difficulties, and paralysis. Patients may also experience changes in blood pressure and heart rate. Despite intensive medical care, the mortality rate for tetanus remains between 10% and 20%. Most individuals who develop tetanus will begin to notice symptoms within 14 days of infection. Anyone who is not vaccinated against tetanus is at risk of contracting the disease. Tetanus occurs worldwide and can affect individuals of all ages. It is more prevalent in rural and agricultural areas where contact with soil or manure is more likely, and in regions with inadequate immunization coverage. Travelers engaging in humanitarian aid work, such as construction or demolition, may be at increased risk if they are not vaccinated. In the United States, rare cases of tetanus occur primarily in individuals who have not received the full series of recommended tetanus vaccinations or who have not kept up with their 10-year booster shots. Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent tetanus. Tetanus vaccines are combination vaccines that protect against tetanus and diphtheria, and some also protect against pertussis (whooping cough). For infants and children, the CDC recommends three doses of the DTaP vaccine to build strong immunity against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis. These doses should be administered at 2 months, 4 months, and 6 months of age. Young children then require two booster doses to maintain protection, given at 15–18 months and 4–6 years of age. For preteens, a single dose of the Tdap vaccine is recommended between the ages of 11 and 12 to boost immunity. Teenagers who did not receive the Tdap vaccine as preteens should get a dose during their next visit to a healthcare provider. All adults should receive a tetanus booster shot every 10 years after their most recent dose during adolescence. Adults who have never received the Tdap vaccine should get one dose, followed by either a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years. Healthcare providers can administer the Tdap vaccine to any adult who has never received it, regardless of when they last received a Td booster. Prompt first aid is crucial for all wounds, even minor ones such as blisters, scrapes, or any break in the skin. If washing the wound is not possible, an alcohol-based hand rub can be used as an alternative.
